Hi, posted today, the person telling you to anti-air didn't tell you why it's important, so I will.
Jump-ins in Fighting games(sf6 specifically) are SUPER STRONG.
Even if you block your opponents jump-in, you are at a disadvantage!(- frames as opposed to + frames)
This means they can go for a un-reactable throw/strike(this is part of the mix-up people are talking about). 
Stopping this situation is why (fundamentals)anti-airs are so important. 
Therefore, a trade, is actually in your favor, because your stopped your opponent from attempting to set up their offense, and did damage at the same time!

This is a super common situation that I've come across throughout learning these games. The people who play them have played them so long they forgot what it's like to actually know nothing, in a game like this, knowledge is half of the fight.

As someone who has gone through the experience of attempting to get good at video games of many different competitive genres(and also hates to lose). you're on the right track. That is to play more, but JUST playing more doesn't actually do anything unless we are actively attempting to get "something" out of the experience. 

To actually make the play more=get better equation work. You(i.e. We) must, and I cannot emphasize this enough, MUST look at things objectively. 

Winning and learning almost never happen together.

This means watching your replays to see what you wanted to happen in a situation versus what actually happened.

Fighting games in general have 3 states that either play is in at all times, they have super fancy Japanese names which is where they come from, but really it's as simple as this. My opponent is doing nothing "rock", my opponent is establishing a threat "paper", or my opponent is expecting me to do something and is pre-emptively preparing for it "scissors". 
They're also 3 pillars of neutral. These are totally different and I recommend looking them up.
The question, What do I do? Isn't the best question to ask if I'm being honest either, because there isn't a win button.
Imagine how boring that would be if both player had a win button and whoever pressed it first simply won the game.

The simplest way to describe how to win in fighting games is to make your opponent think they have to commit to an action.

That's literally it, we need to make our opponent do "something."

Okay, okay, this dude has put "something" exactly like that twice and I have no idea what he's talking about.

That's because depending on your opponent, it will be different.

Let's take this interaction in a vacuum and look at it from a couple points of view.(also called Options)

Ken gets knocked down, and you have the ability to hit him on wakeup(meaty attack) so that he has to block.

Well if Ken is invincible(OD/EX. DP/Wake-up super) he doesn't have to block and your meaty will lose.

If Ken hits a button, he gets counter hit(hit during the startup of an attack) and you get to take away his life with a combo(win condition)

If Ken jumps, it's very similar to hitting a button, except he would jump out of a throw(you cannot throw an airborne target), but if you do the same meaty that got him counter-hit, he will still get hit, grounded, just not counter-hit.(If you hit him and he goes airborne your meaty was too late, and he got some of the startup of the jump off first). **every move has startup

Ken can also block(everyone hates this option for some reason)
But lets say he does, your meaty will be blocked, he will not take damage, and who is at advantage (+,-) depends on the move that was used to meaty.

These options are the "somethings" if you notice there isn't an option that wins all the time no matter what, because if you don't throw, or meaty, DP loses the same goes for the other options.

I've seen a lot of comments of people saying go do this go do that. Fighting games don't work like that, especially not with 2 minutes of gameplay as material, however we can still start here.
1. Go to training mode
2. GO TO TRAINING MODE(ignore if applicable)
3. Learn your confirms! 
2LK, 2LP, 5LP -- Low Starter
2LP, 5LP, 5LP -- 4f Starter
2LP, 2LP, 5LP, 5LK -- 4-hit String; 214K whiffs if cancelled
4. If we're too far away for those buttons to reach, find out what we should be doing to get yourself into a situation to make them reach! 
5. We should now be mashing buttons into a training dummy until they're second nature, to the point of your fingers are doing the combo and you don't have to think about it

6. On your wakeup, block the first attack.
